docs.title: Roster
docs.text:
Built-in registry: Responder (Haiku, fast triage, own prompt dir), Analyst (Sonnet, default investigator, Analyst.md), Architect (Opus, persona on the Analyst base).

Frontmatter personas shipped in agents/ (non-exhaustive; each is definition + optional prompt dir): AssistedAnalyst, QuickAnalyst, SeniorAnalyst, StaffAnalyst, Laconic + L1Laconic, Challenger + ChallengerSonnet, Scout, Ops, Craftsman, Explain, IncidentReporter, IncidentFilterBuilder, OnCallConfigBuilder, ChannelSummary, SlackListener, Sentinel, Watch, Workflow, TaskBuilder, CreateSkill / ValidateSkill / Eval, Synthesis, Scratch, GapMapper (+ its referee GapReferee), PRRiskScorer, and the memory pair ExecLearningsAgent + MemoryAssimilator (see MEMORY_SYSTEM.md).

docs.title: Depth tiers (what the UIs actually ask for)
docs.text:
The UIs do not name agents. neubird-ui's prompt-bar depth picker and falcon-app's composer mode chip both send a tier alias in the request's agent field, and internal/agents/tiers.go decides what it stands for:

Tier Agent Intent Ask QuickAnalyst Answer and hand off, rather than investigate Assisted AssistedAnalyst Bounded progress, then hand the next step back to the user L1 L1Laconic Bounded investigation, driven to a conclusion — Laconic's doctrine on Opus 5.5 at low thinking effort (the model rejects a thinking disable) L2 Laconic The same investigation with extended thinking on (high effort) L3 Challenger Self-refuting deep analysis on Opus
  • Owning the table here is the point: retargeting a tier is a falcon change, not a coordinated release of two UIs. Before this, falcon-app's L1 meant Laconic while neubird-ui's meant Analyst.
  • Not every UI offers every tier. Assisted appears in neubird-ui's agent list only, behind the enableAssistedTier ConfigCat flag, and falcon-app never sends it. That is a decision about who is offered a depth, not about which aliases resolve: falcon answers Assisted for anyone who sends it, so the flag cannot desync from a rollout. It sits between Ask and L1 — it investigates, unlike Ask, but stops at six tool rounds with structured follow-ups instead of driving to an answer, which is why it is its own tier rather than a cheaper L1.
  • Aliases are reserved and matched case-insensitively. resolveAgent consults the tier table before the registry, so an agent (or raven row) named L2 is unreachable by name — TestTierTargetsAreShippedAgents fails the build if one appears.
  • Concrete agent names still work on the same field: Sentinel, the builder agents and raven-authored agents are unaffected.
  • The session is stamped with the resolved agent (def.Name), so a run started as L2 is recorded and filterable as Laconic.
  • L1 and L2 are two agents rather than one agent at two thinking settings on purpose. Model and thinking can only be pinned per agent name (AGENT_MODEL_OVERRIDES, the one lever that outranks a deployment-wide ConfigCat InferenceModelOverride — note frontmatter model: is the weakest signal, see InferenceModelLabel), and a distinct name is what makes an L1 run distinguishable from an L2 one in session metadata, agent-name filters and evals. L1Laconic shares Laconic's doctrine via prompt_dir: (one copy of the SOUL), the same arrangement ChallengerSonnet has with Challenger; TestLaconicTiersDifferOnlyByThinking fails the build if the pair drifts apart.
  • FALCON_AGENT_TIERS retargets tiers without a rebuild: l3=DeepAnalyst,l1=Analyst. Unlisted tiers keep their defaults; a malformed or unknown entry is logged and ignored rather than emptying a tier. Per deployment, the same value goes in the agent_tiers key of the llms ConfigCat squad JSON (raven forwards it top-level; FetchLLMEnv maps it to the env var set-if-empty, so a pod-level env var still wins). Like llm_tier, it is read at boot — restart falcon after changing the flag.

docs.title: Core Agent Loop
docs.text:
Entry points: agent.Run (fire-and-forget goroutine) → agent.Execute → executeInternal → runLoop. All in internal/ai/agent.go.

flowchart TD
    EX["Execute(ctx, session, def, prompt, cb, cfg)"] --> MEMPRE["Pre-load long-term memory from ACE<br/>ensureMemoryLoaded(prompt) — unless cfg.DisableMemory"]
    MEMPRE --> TO["Own the timeout: WithoutCancel(parent) + def.Timeout<br/>AfterFunc propagates real cancellations"]
    TO --> EI[executeInternal]

    EI --> RESOLVE["Resolve per-run state (fresh runState)<br/>• transport for def.Model<br/>• tool + skill allowlists (def / cfg)<br/>• base prompt: prompt-dir OR persona-on-Analyst.md<br/>• ContextSections → frozen memory prompt sections<br/>• citations, cost cap, structured-output state"]
    RESOLVE --> PROMPTASM["buildPrompt = PromptAssembler(persona, date, base,<br/>schema, table, learnings, memory-tools, tool-hints,<br/>insights, citation-discipline, write-todos, skills)"]
    PROMPTASM --> USERMSG["Append user message<br/>(downscaled attachments, quick-budget prep)"]
    USERMSG --> LOOP

    subgraph LOOP ["runLoop — one iteration per LLM turn, cap 100 (200 for pipeline RCA)"]
        TSTART["Turn start:<br/>• ctx / cost-cap check<br/>• maybeInjectSteer (queued /v1/infer/steer notes)"]
        TSTART --> FILTER["Per-turn tool filter (see Tool system)"]
        FILTER --> MSGS["messagesForAPI: doc offload → trim → ACE history tiers<br/>(see Context management)"]
        MSGS --> SEND["SendMessageStream(system, msgs, tools)<br/>stream: text→OnText, tool_use→OnToolExec"]
        SEND --> ERR{error / empty?}
        ERR -->|"transient stream error<br/>or empty response"| RETRY["bounded retry, turn not counted"]
        RETRY --> TSTART
        ERR -->|ok| STOP{stop_reason}
        STOP -->|tool_use| EXEC["executeTools → append tool_result user msg<br/>record TurnSnapshot, per-turn tools rollup,<br/>launch background interim summarizer"]
        EXEC --> BUDGET{"evidence rounds ≥ MaxToolRounds?"}
        BUDGET -->|yes| QF["quick-finalization nudge:<br/>tools narrowed to finalization set"]
        BUDGET -->|no| TSTART
        QF --> TSTART
        STOP -->|max_tokens| CONT["inject 'continue where you left off'"] --> TSTART
        STOP -->|end_turn| ENDCHK
    end

    ENDCHK{"end_turn checks"} -->|"no text at all"| NUDGE["zero-text nudge (bounded);<br/>exhausted → noTextExhausted, fall through"]
    NUDGE --> LOOP
    ENDCHK -->|"open todos"| TODO["todo-completion nudge (bounded)"] --> LOOP
    ENDCHK -->|clean| POST["Post-pass:<br/>thin-answer → conclusion call (prose-only)"]
    POST --> SYNTH{"Synthesis dispatch (executeInternal)"}
    SYNTH -->|"IsHealthAssessment + ≥3 sources"| HS[runHealthSynthesis]
    SYNTH -->|"IsCostAnalysis + ≥2 sources"| CS[runCostSynthesis]
    SYNTH -->|"reportPassApplies (≥1 source, synthesis not disabled,<br/>not a structured-output agent)"| OS["runSynthesis — report pass on the run's own model,<br/>reusing the loop's cached prefix<br/>→ runConfidencePass (scores the report)"]
    SYNTH -->|otherwise| PLAIN["loop answer is final"]
    HS --> DONE
    CS --> DONE
    OS --> DONE
    PLAIN --> DONE["Progress done · cost to span · saveACEHistory ·<br/>compressOldHistory · rating request · OnDone"]

Notes that the diagram compresses:

  • Timeout contract (unchanged, load-bearing): Execute strips the parent deadline via context.WithoutCancel, then applies TIMEOUT_SECONDS env (the squad's investigation_timeout_seconds) → def.Timeout → 10 min. context.AfterFunc still honours explicit cancellation. Never pass a deadline-bearing context — a parent deadline firing first is indistinguishable from a user cancel and misclassifies the run as CANCELLED. Callers set def.Timeout instead.
  • Deadline recovery — a timed-out run never ends as a bare failure. When the deadline fires and a synthesis pass qualifies, synthesis runs on synthesisContext — a fresh budget from context.Background() with its own 3-minute cap (only explicit user cancel propagates in). When no synthesis qualifies, runTimeoutSummary forces a terminal wrap-up on the same fresh-context mechanism: one tools-less call on the run's own model producing a final summary (streamed, appended to history, stored via rs.synthesisText with a time-limit caveat, PROMPT_STATUS_COMPLETED); if that call fails, the floor persists the already-gathered narrative (collectAssistantText) with the caveat. Only when even the floor is empty does the run surface as FAILED with the plain timeout note. Structured-output agents (ends_with_structured_output) skip the prose wrap-up (it would fight their emit flow), as do agents with disable_synthesis set (e.g. Watch, Sentinel) — they rely on terse, machine-parseable output rather than prose, so they keep the plain timeout note instead. Worst-case wall clock is therefore def.Timeout + up to 3 min of wrap-up.
  • Deferred web_search: a tool_use turn can carry an unpaired server_tool_use (Anthropic defers the search so client tools run first). The continuation turn must send back only tool_results with the unpaired block intact, so the quick-finalization transition is skipped/deferred on that turn (resolveDeferredSearch, pendingQuickFinalization).
  • Confidence machinery: a run is scored once, at the end, by runConfidencePass (agent.go): after the report pass writes the report, one more call on the same prefix plus the report asks for a single CONFIDENCE: NN line against a fixed rubric (confidenceRequestText). That score is recorded on the ProgressTracker and is what the PDF, the turn snapshot, raven upload and the Langfuse final_confidence / confidence_source: report_pass metadata carry. There is no model-facing confidence tool and no confidence nudge. The interim summarizer does not set the run's confidence: an earlier design fed its score to the tracker, but it saw only a delta and never the report, and its last guess became the run's permanent confidence. Consequences: the tracker's confidence — and so progress.confidence and interim_summary.confidence — is 0 for the whole run until the report pass scores it; runs that end without a report pass (no sources, disable_synthesis, structured-output agents, health/cost synthesis) fall back to completionConfidenceFloor (75) at SetDone, and the Langfuse final_confidence is then omitted because the floor is not a judgment. One legacy exception: emitServerToolDone records a flat 70 when a server-side web_search returns URLs and nothing has scored yet, so a run that used web search shows 70 mid-run, and keeps it if no report pass follows. Live (provisional) confidence: the summarizer ends each update with a provisional score on the same bands, emitted as interim_summary.provisional_confidence. It is display-only — never recorded on the tracker, never stored, never the final score.
  • Cost cap: checked at the top of each turn from the context's cost accumulator. The turn that crosses the cap completes; the next one doesn't start. costCapExceeded injects a framing note so synthesis explicitly says the investigation is incomplete.
  • Empty-response and stream retries share a bounded budget with backoff and do not consume iterations; the budget deliberately does not reset on thinking-only turns so a persistently silent model can't farm fresh retries out of the no-text nudge cycle.
  • Iteration cap (100 per batch, 200 for pipeline RCA stages, or cfg.MaxIterations): the loop asks for a summary (requestSummary), fires OnContinuePrompt, and blocks until Continue() — server/auto-continue callers keep going, TUI asks the user.
  • After the loop, structured-output agents run their own save/confirmation gates (ensureIncidentFilterSaveConfirmation, QuickAnalyst/AssistedAnalyst handoffs) instead of the generic nudges.

docs.title: Tool system
docs.text:
Three layers, resolved at different lifetimes:

flowchart TD
    subgraph L1 ["1 · Registry (NewAgent, per agent lifetime)"]
        BUILT["Built-ins (BuildTools) + tool_search"]
        RP["write_todos — always appended"]
        WS["web_search (server tool, ENABLE_WEBSEARCH)"]
        ACET["ACE MCP tools/list<br/>memory stubs excluded from 'existing' map<br/>⇒ ACE overrides save_learnings /<br/>load_relevant_learnings / update_memory"]
        META["ACE _meta flags:<br/>HiddenFromLLM → session-callable only<br/>AgentRestricted → allowlist-only<br/>Deferred → tool_search-gated"]
        LMCP["Local MCP servers + local CLIs + devtools code_task"]
    end

    subgraph L2 ["2 · Per-run allowlists (executeInternal)"]
        DEFT["def.Tools:<br/>no '*' → EXCLUSIVE (rs.allowedTools)<br/>with '*' → additive unlock (rs.unlockedTools)<br/>['none'] → zero tools<br/>empty → all unrestricted"]
        CFGT["cfg.AllowedTools: exclusive; may only narrow def's boundary"]
        DENY["rs.deniedTools (subtractive):<br/>DisableMemory → all memory tools<br/>DisableListTables, DisableWriteTodos"]
        CIT["EnableCitations unlocks citation tools last<br/>(cannot be overwritten by cfg)"]
    end

    subgraph L3 ["3 · Per-turn filter (runLoop, every turn)"]
        DENYF[deny-list first] --> PDF["doc query tools only when a PDF is present<br/>(then force-included even under exclusive lists)"]
        PDF --> VIZ["chart tools gated until visualizations skill loaded<br/>(explicit allowlist bypasses)"]
        VIZ --> DEFR["Deferred tools withheld until exposed via tool_search<br/>(AgentRestricted + explicitly listed bypasses)"]
        DEFR --> AR["AgentRestricted → only if unlocked/allowed<br/>unrestricted → unless exclusive list omits"]
        AR --> ORDER["append-only ordering + citation tool pinned last<br/>+ single cache breakpoint on the last tool"]
    end

    L1 --> L2 --> L3 --> LLMREQ["tools[] on this turn's API request"]

Execution side (executeTools → executeTool): built-ins dispatch by name in a big switch; anything else routes to its recorded MCP session via mcpSessions[name]. MCP results are text-content joined then JSON-parsed — a tool "error" is (text, isErr=true), not a transport error. SQL errors trigger auto-learning (autoSaveColumnLearning, autoSaveGroupByLearning) and a MANDATORY save_learnings nudge appended to the tool output. Tool outputs are truncated for context (truncateForContext), summarized for the TUI (summarizeToolData), and counted into RecordDataRead only when isDataTool — memory/meta/bookkeeping tools are excluded by name.

docs.title: Background tool calls
docs.text:
A tool call normally blocks its turn. A tool that sets Backgroundable may be started detached: the engine returns a placeholder tool_result immediately, runs the call on the run's context, and delivers the real output as text on a later turn. Delivery is automatic; each call also gets a short handle (bg_N) named in its placeholder and its delivery header (with the call's arguments and, on claims and pipeline runs, its call_idx), so the model can tell calls of one tool apart and aim wait_for_workers or cancel_workers at a single call. Two routes reach the detached path, and Backgroundable gates both: the model asks, by setting a background boolean the tool declares on its own schema; or the tool's own BackgroundDefault reads the call's arguments and says this shape always detaches. The second exists because a prompt is a suggestion — a tool whose contract already pins how a call runs should not depend on the model remembering a flag — and it keeps per-tool policy in the tool rather than the engine.

A third route is the deployment switch (FALCON_TOOL_BACKGROUNDING_ENABLED), which also promotes a call that simply outlives FALCON_TOOL_BACKGROUND_AFTER_MS — adopting the in-flight call where it is rather than killing and retrying it. That route is an allowlist: only calls that leave falcon for a customer system (toolHitsCustomerSystem, the same rule classifyTool uses to label a call with the service it queried), minus schema probing (backgroundSchemaLookup). Bare ACE names — memory, inventory, skills, incident and alert writes — are orchestration the next turn is built from, and a detached write can be cancelled mid-flight and then reported as having produced nothing; neither belongs off the turn. backgroundExcluded names the handful that must finish regardless of how they are declared. The promotion placeholder says how long the call had already run; a flagged one does not, and both carry the per-tool bound (boundDetachedCall) unless the tool's own BackgroundDefault claims this call.

Local dev builds turn this on by default: make build / make build-dev compile with -tags localdev (LOCALDEV_TAGS), which flips the default of FALCON_TOOL_BACKGROUNDING_ENABLED to on (localdev_on.go). An explicit value always wins (=false turns it off); release (-tags release), server (-tags debug), CI eval builds and go test never set the tag. Every run states its agent and mode once, before the first turn (runinfo.go): the log line agent run starting agent=… model=… timeout=… tool_backgrounding=on promote_after=42s session=… (Info, so server pods show it without --debug), and the same key=value line as a header in the TUI (AgentCallback.OnRunStart; on in local dev builds, FALCON_SHOW_RUN_INFO overrides). In the TUI without --debug, slog output is discarded (main.go sends log to io.Discard, and the default slog handler writes through log), so the background-tool log lines above need --debug there. TUI tool cards match results by tool_use id, so a backgrounded call that finishes after a newer call of the same tool completes its own card.

It is deadline-bounded, not fire-and-forget. When the model stops calling tools, joinBackgroundBeforeAnswer waits for every outstanding call, hands them over as a user turn and takes one more loop iteration, so the answer is written with that evidence rather than without it. The wait has no budget of its own: the investigation's end-to-end deadline is already on the loop's context (executeInternal runs on execCtx, from resolveExecuteTimeout), so waiting on it is the same thing as respecting it. Nothing is dropped for being slow — only for the investigation running out of time, and then the model is told what it lost. That is safe because answer writing is not bounded by the same deadline: on DeadlineExceeded, synthesis and runTimeoutSummary both run on a fresh, deadline-independent context.

maxBackgroundJoinRounds bounds rounds, not time — a further round only happens if the model started more work while being held. Past it the gate stops waiting but not reporting: it delivers whatever finished and names whatever it drops, once. The handover preamble is gated on endsWithStructuredOutput, so an agent that finishes through a completion tool is not steered into prose.

Each call runs on its own child of the run context, and abandoning it cancels that child — a flag alone would leave a goroutine inside executeTool writing to rs and to the agent's MCP and large-result state. Any exit that bypasses the gate (terminal tool, iteration cap, cost cap, fatal error, cancelled context) calls abandonBackground, which cancels and then waits up to backgroundTeardownGrace for the goroutines to leave before synthesis and MCP teardown read that state. A tool that ignores its context is logged and left rather than hanging the run.

The real output is re-recorded against the original tool_use id, so a citation on a backgrounded call verifies against what the tool returned rather than against the placeholder. See background_tools.go.

ACE MCP transports are never reused across prompts: each one is opened by NewAgent or openAndConnectACE and closed by ReleaseMCPSession when the prompt completes. ACE's session id manager accepts an id it no longer knows (an ACE restart, or a request served by another replica) with a 200 rather than a 404, and the connect_database that follows then registers the project's external tools onto a session ACE never initialized — logging each failure server-side and still reporting success, leaving the prompt with the static tool set and no integrations. Connection reuse instead lives one layer down, in the shared MCP HTTP transport (tools_mcp.go: sharedMCPHTTPClient, newMCPRoundTripper). Project scoping is session state: connect_database({database: projectUUID}), never a tool parameter.

docs.title: Context management (short-term memory)
docs.text:
Everything the model "remembers" inside and across turns of a session:

flowchart TD
    SESS["Session.Messages — append-only, thread-safe<br/>(user / assistant / tool_result turns)"]
    SESS --> MFA[messagesForAPI — every turn]

    subgraph MFA_PIPE [messagesForAPI pipeline]
        OFF["1 · offloadLargeDocuments<br/>big PDFs/docs → compact placeholder + docProjection;<br/>viewed PDF pages re-injected from run-durable accumulator;<br/>queryable via search_document / read_document /<br/>view_pdf_pages (PDF present, or text doc on an agent naming them) or code_exec doc_id: (text)"]
        OFF --> TRIM["2 · trimMessages(current, budget)<br/>compress oldest tool_results, then drop oldest messages;<br/>didCompact → OnCompacting"]
        TRIM --> HIST["3 · prior-session history budget =<br/>min(historyBudget, totalBudget − current)"]
        HIST --> TIERS{buildACEHistoryMessages}
        TIERS -->|fits| T1["Tier 1 — full turns incl. tool_use/tool_result blocks;<br/>past tool_use ids hydrated for citation verification"]
        TIERS -->|tight| T2["Tier 2/3 — compressed prompt + answer text;<br/>attachments preserved; lightweight RCA index only"]
    end

    MFA --> NORM["normalize/repair: unpaired tool_use, stale thinking blocks,<br/>server-tool blocks downgraded to text when the tool<br/>isn't declared this turn (serializeServerToolBlocksOnly)"]
    NORM --> CACHE["stampCacheCheckpoint — prompt-cache anchors"]
    CACHE --> API[API request messages]

    SESS -. "between investigations" .-> COMP["compressOldHistory:<br/>prior investigations' tool exchanges →<br/>compact summaries (compressForHistory)"]
    SESS -. "end of run" .-> SAVE["saveACEHistory: TurnSnapshots + messages<br/>→ ACE (durable conversation history)"]
    SAVE -.-> LOAD["next session: LoadACEHistory → a.aceHistory<br/>→ tiers above"]

So the memory hierarchy, in one line each:

Horizon Mechanism Lives in This turn streamed response + tool_results wire This investigation Session.Messages, trimmed/offloaded per turn process memory Earlier investigations, same session compressOldHistory summaries process memory Prior sessions ACE conversation history, injected at tier 1/2/3 ACE Cross-session knowledge learnings/insights (assimilated store) ACE — see MEMORY_SYSTEM.md Local caches/queues internal/{history,feedback} jsonl in ~/.config/neubird disk (cache, not source of truth) In-process learning cache internal/{learnings,tablelearnings} process memory — ConfigDB is the durable copy

docs.title: Agent struct — shared vs per-run state
docs.text:
agent is long-lived; runState is created fresh per Execute and never shared, which is what makes concurrent Execute calls on one agent safe.

Shared fields are immutable after NewAgent or carry their own synchronisation:

Field Type Protection Notes baseCfg ProviderConfig immutable LLM provider credentials basePromptSection, schemaSection, extraSection, tableSection, insightsSection, toolHintsSection, skillsSection *MutableSection sync.RWMutex inside Prompt sections; memory-derived ones are updated by the learning caches skills skillsRegistry sync.RWMutex inside All loaded local skills mcp mcpRegistry sync.RWMutex inside Tool list + sessions; sealCache marks the cache anchor sentinel / watch managers sync.Mutex + atomics Background monitor lifecycles digestTransport Transport WaitGroup drain before close Shared by all Haiku digest calls interim interimState sync.Mutex + sync.WaitGroup Background summarizer state lastResult safeRunResult sync.RWMutex Outcome of most recent Execute ace aceConnector sync.Mutex + atomic.Int64 Reconnect deduplication memorySeenIDs, sqlLearnings, … maps dedicated mutexes Long-term-memory local caches agentName atomic.Value atomic Set by TUI, read by agent goroutine

Per-run (runState): transport, buildPrompt closure, resolved allow/deny/unlock maps, progress tracker, turn snapshots, sources, charts, doc projection, structured-output state, counters. Fresh per call; closed/discarded on return.

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
1. Per-Execute transport (rs.transport) — fresh per call for the main loop; carries model, debug log; closed on return. Fully isolated.
  2. Digest transport (a.digestTransport) — created once in NewAgent, reused for all background interim-summary calls; closed in Close() only after interim.wg.Wait() drains in-flight goroutines.

docs.title: Background interim summarizer
docs.text: After each tool round, launchBackgroundSummarizer sends a snapshot copy of the current investigation's history to Haiku and emits a rolling "what we know so far" via OnInterimSummary. Invariants: one goroutine at a time (bgRunning under interimState.mu), rate-limited to one launch per 10 s, wg.Add(1) inside the mutex so Close() can never race a starting goroutine, stale results dropped via a generation counter, disabled for health/cost runs and disable_interim_summary agents. It never sets the run's confidence; its only score is the display-only provisional_confidence (see Confidence machinery).

docs.title: Prompt sections and lazySection

docs.title: Verified RCA Pipeline — Working Design Document
docs.text:
Goal: Design a concrete implementation, grounded in falcon's actual code, of a multi-stage verified-RCA pipeline:

  1. Context setup agent (TelemetryRecon — already created in agents/TelemetryRecon*)
  2. Hypothesis producer (investigator) — must emit structured output (RCA evidence contract: hypothesis ledger, onset timestamps, citations)
  3. Verifier — fresh context, refutes against the contract, structured verdict
  4. Judge / gate — mechanical checks in Go where possible; bounded retry loop

Also answer: does this need subagents? How does it compare to what Cursor does?

Motivating evidence: 5 investigations of incident 93dd10ab (swimlanemirror, Aug 15 queue backlog): only 1 of 5 (run A) found the verified root cause (producer surge vs 32-pod KEDA ceiling). The 4 wrong runs all: anchored on loud ES-master signals, never measured producer rate, cited post-peak evidence as cause, and passed citation verification anyway. Full analysis in the conversation of 2026-08-16/17; key traces in ~/Downloads/trace_*.json.

docs.title: Evidence continuity — the ledger (added 2026-08-18)
docs.text:
Six shipped bugs shared one cause: the citable tool-call catalog was scoped to a single Execute while the pipeline's evidence spans stages (recon → investigator rounds → nudges → fix-ups). Each incident was patched locally (offline validation flags, citation merging, prompt boundaries) until the class was closed structurally: ai.EvidenceLedger, one per pipeline run, passed via RunConfig to every PRODUCER stage. Each producer Execute seeds its catalog from the ledger and mirrors new calls back, so cited_tool_call_idx values are continuous across recon and all correction rounds — contracts cite recon's measurements directly, carried indices survive full in-loop validation, and OfflineContractValidation was deleted. The verifier NEVER shares the ledger: the referee re-executes cited queries in a fresh evidence world — that independence is the product. Vocabulary note: "onset from the data" now includes recon's data; the investigator re-measures only for fresh values or doubted numbers.

Judge note: stage [G]+[2] is the judge for single runs. A separate LLM "judge" only appears in the ensemble variant: N parallel investigator asks → Merger adjudicates by contract score, never majority (our 5-run sample: majority elects the wrong RCA 4:1).

docs.title: AlertCorrelator-inspired principles (added 2026-08-17 at ganesh's direction)
docs.text:
agents/AlertCorrelator/SOUL.md is the production-proven template for structure+evidence discipline. Lifted into this design:

  1. Per-claim evidence gate: every ledger row and the root cause carry an evidence: []string list of concrete named signals (entities, timestamps, values) plus a citation — mirroring alerts[].evidence. "A claim you cannot back with valid evidence is not confirmed."
  2. Completeness roster: the contract gains alerts[] — every alert in the incident, exactly once, with disposition: explained_by_root_cause | separate_issue | unexplained + evidence for explained members. A root cause that silently ignores half the incident's alerts fails validation (mirrors "return every input alert exactly once; never drop one").
  3. Judgment vs hard boundaries: investigator/verifier SOULs follow AlertCorrelator's shape — judgment is free ("not a recipe"), but a Hard boundaries (not judgment calls) section + closing Non-negotiables checklist state the mechanical invariants (cause ≤ symptom onset, all ledger classes terminated, evidence per claim, ids verbatim).
  4. Vocabulary note — the contract's "onset from the data, not alert metadata" and the time-anchor principle "the alert/ticket record is authoritative for WHEN" are compatible, not in tension: the fetched alert/ticket record pins the symptom onset and the query windows (it IS citable data — you fetched it), while cause onsets come from the backing telemetry series. "Not alert metadata" forbids trusting unverified enrichment prose, not the record's own fire/filing timestamp.
  5. Exhaustive output spec: exact JSON example + field notes + "required always, even when false/[]" + honest confidence semantics ("the pipeline may gate on this, so judge it honestly").
  6. Precision over recall: a narrow verified RCA beats a broad unverified one; when evidence doesn't clear the gate, say unexplained rather than stretch.
  7. Delivery discipline: the terminal emit_result(rca.contract.v1) IS the delivery — final action, reasoning in earlier turns.

All five ledger classes REQUIRED (Go check for class coverage) — this alone rejects runs B/C/D/E (empty input_increased row). Confirmed/refuted rows require measurement + evidence + citation (per-claim evidence gate). alerts[] roster: every incident alert exactly once; explained_by_root_cause members require evidence (completeness invariant).

docs.title: Go mechanical gate (new internal/ai/contract.go)
docs.text:
Checks (all domain-agnostic, no LLM):

  1. root_cause.onset_utc <= symptom.onset_utc (kills C/E post-hoc causes)
  2. every ledger class present, none "blocked" without blocked_reason naming what was tried
  3. every citation_idx exists in toolCalls; cited result contains the onset timestamps claimed (extends T3 check)
  4. PromQL lint on cited queries: aggregation without cluster/env label while alert labels contain one → violation (kills D's diluted avg)
  5. arithmetic_closure non-empty and mentions both an inflow and a drain figure Failure → synthetic tool-result feedback into the still-open loop (same mechanism as schema validation failure), so the investigator fixes it in-session. Cheap, no new context.

docs.title: RcaVerifier agent (new agents/RcaVerifier.md + SOUL.md)
docs.text:
• Fresh ask, context: [] (no session inheritance — C→B contagion showed why), small tool set: read-only query tools ONLY for spot re-execution of cited queries, no discovery tools.
  • Input: the contract JSON + resolved citation excerpts. NOT the investigator transcript (prevents anchor inheritance).
  • SOUL: "You are a referee. Attempt to refute: (a) re-run 2-3 load-bearing cited queries verbatim; (b) check each refuted/blocked ledger row was genuinely attempted; (c) hunt internal contradictions; (d) default to fail on uncertainty."
  • ends_with_structured_output: {pass: bool, violations: [{code, detail, ledger_class?}], reexecution_results: []}.

docs.title: Orchestration: where the pipeline runner lives
docs.text: Two options, recommend (a): (a) Server-side chain in askAce (internal/server): if agent def has pre_context_agent/verify_with, askAce runs the sub-asks sequentially, threading outputs. ~200 LoC; reuses everything (sessions, tracing, cost caps). Each stage is its own trace (falcon.ask children) — evaluable independently. (b) Merlin-side: FalconSubmit issues 3 sequential asks. More moving parts, crosses repo boundary, but zero falcon changes. Rejected for latency of iteration.

docs.title: Retry budget & failure posture
docs.text:
• gate/verifier rounds: ≤2 each. On exhaustion do NOT block the report: publish with banner UNVERIFIED: <violations> + confidence forced to low. An SRE seeing a wrong-but-flagged report beats silence.
  • Cost: recon (~$0.3, small model) + verifier (~$0.5) on top of ~$4 investigations; ~20% overhead. Ensemble mode (3×investigator + Merger) reserved for high-risk incidents.

docs.title: Acceptance test (already owned)
docs.text: Replay incident 93dd10ab: gate+verifier must REJECT the B/C/D/E contracts (each for its specific violation: post-hoc cause / empty input row / diluted agg / unmeasured publish rate) and PASS A's. Then N fresh runs with pipeline on → measure convergence to producer-surge RCA. Evals live in evals/ (existing harness).

docs.title: Why coding agents (Cursor) feel accurate — and what transfers
docs.text:
Cursor does NOT run hypothesis→verifier→judge chains. Its architecture (public info as of early 2026): single agent loop + strong retrieval (codebase embedding index), a specialized apply/diff model, and — the decisive part — cheap objective verifiers supplied by the environment: compiler, type-checker, linters, tests. The agent iterates against ground truth that costs milliseconds and never lies. Accuracy comes from tight feedback loops with an oracle, not from multi-agent structure.

RCA has no compiler. The design above is therefore manufacturing the oracle: the mechanical gate (timestamps, ledger completeness, citation time-ranges, agg-scope lint) is the "type-checker for causal claims", and the verifier's query re-execution is the "test run". Subagents are needed only where fresh context matters (verifier independence, recon isolation) — the gate itself is plain Go and free. That's the honest answer to "does this need subagents": two extra asks per investigation, yes; but the biggest correctness win (the mechanical gate) needs none.

docs.title: Session notes / how to resume
docs.text:
• TelemetryRecon agent already exists (created earlier today): agents/TelemetryRecon.md + TelemetryRecon/{IDENTITY,SOUL}.md; go test ./internal/agents/ green.
  • If resuming after interruption: check Task checklist above; T9 (skeleton code) is the only open item and needs user go-ahead.
  • Line numbers above are approximate (agent.go is ~13k lines); re-grep span names ("falcon.sonnet_loop", "falcon.opus_synthesis") to relocate.

docs.title: Environment Variables
docs.text: On startup, Falcon loads env vars from the following files in order — earlier sources win: .env (cwd), ~/.hawkeye.env, ~/.neubird.env, ~/.falcon.env. All files are optional. Variables already set in the environment always take precedence.

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Variable Description ANTHROPIC_API_KEY Anthropic API key. Required when LLM_PROVIDER is anthropic or when no Bedrock credentials are set.

docs.title: Optional

Required when using Bedrock with IAM credentials. BEDROCK_AWS_REGION us-west-2 AWS region for Bedrock API calls. BEDROCK_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY — AWS secret access key. Required when using Bedrock with IAM credentials. LLM_PROVIDER auto-detect LLM provider: anthropic or bedrock. Auto-detected from available credentials if not set.

docs.text: Flag Short Type Default Description --assess -a bool — Automatically run a health assessment immediately after connecting. --help -h bool — Show help and exit. --profile — string — Use a named login profile. Defaults to the unnamed profile. --version -v bool — Print version information and exit. --window — duration 1h Lookback window for health assessments. Use as --window=<duration>, e.g. --window=4h. Accepts Go duration strings: 15m, 1h, 24h.

docs.text:
Arguments:

docs.title: Agent Personas
docs.text: NeuBird includes three built-in agent personas, each powered by a different Claude model optimized for a specific trade-off between speed and reasoning depth.

docs.title: Personas
docs.text: Persona Model Speed Depth Best for Responder Claude Haiku Fast Light Quick triage, confirming whether an issue is active, getting immediate next actions Analyst Claude Sonnet Balanced Deep Root cause analysis, multi-service investigations, detailed evidence gathering Architect Claude Opus Thorough Maximum Writing runbooks, design reviews, systemic fix proposals, complex cross-service analysis

docs.title: Switching personas
docs.text:
Type /agent to open the persona picker. Use ↑ ↓ to select and Enter to confirm. The switch takes effect immediately — your next question uses the new persona.

You can also switch mid-investigation. If a Responder triage reveals a deeper issue, switch to Analyst for the full RCA.

docs.title: When to use each
docs.text:
Start with Responder when you need speed:

  • "Is the checkout service down right now?"
  • "What's the current error rate on api-gateway?"

Switch to Analyst for investigation:

  • "Why did latency spike at 2am?"
  • "What's causing the increase in 503 errors?"

Escalate to Architect for systemic work:

  • "Write a runbook for handling RDS ACU saturation"
  • "What architectural changes would prevent this class of incident?"

docs.title: Custom personas
docs.text:
Create your own personas by adding .md files to skills/agents/:

---
model: claude-sonnet-5
speed: 2
quality: 2
---

You are a cloud cost specialist. When investigating costs, always break down by service, team, and resource type. Always include a projected monthly cost at the end of your analysis.

The frontmatter sets the model and the speed/quality ratings shown in the picker. The body is appended to the system prompt.

docs.title: Cost Analysis
docs.text: The /cost command analyzes your cloud spending, identifies waste, and projects future costs. NeuBird queries AWS Cost Explorer, Datadog billing data, and resource utilization metrics to produce actionable savings recommendations.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
/cost            # 24-hour lookback (default)
/cost 7d         # 7-day lookback

docs.title: What it analyzes
docs.text:
• Top cost drivers — services ranked by spend with 30-day projections
  • Idle resources — EC2 instances, RDS clusters, and ElastiCache nodes with low utilization
  • Metric cardinality — high-cardinality Datadog metrics driving observability costs
  • Log volume — excessive log output and missing log level filters
  • Over-provisioning — resources sized larger than their actual usage requires

docs.title: Savings categories
docs.text:
The report separates findings into two categories:

Quick Wins — savings achievable with minimal engineering effort (terminate idle instances, adjust tag filters, enable lifecycle policies).

Engineering Projects — larger savings that require code or architecture changes (custom metric cleanup, right-sizing, log restructuring).

Each recommendation includes an estimated monthly savings and effort level.

docs.title: Headless Investigations
docs.text: The neubird run and neubird investigate commands run AI-powered analyses from the command line without the interactive TUI. Designed for programmatic invocation by external tools, CI pipelines, and coding agents like OpenClaw.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
neubird run <capability> --project <name>
neubird run health --project prod_cop
neubird run cost 7d --project prod_cop
neubird investigate "any 403s in the last hour?" --project prod_cop

Findings are printed as markdown to stdout, ending with a Completed in Xs sentinel line. Stderr is used only for errors and the spinner during investigation.

# Save findings to a file
neubird run health --project prod_cop > health-report.md

# Free-form investigation
neubird investigate "what caused the latency spike?" --project prod_cop > findings.md

docs.title: Capabilities
docs.text:
neubird run exposes named analysis types:

Capability Description Default lookback health Full infrastructure health sweep 1 hour cost Cloud cost baseline + 24h spend projection 24 hours investigate Free-form investigation prompt — performance Find latency outliers and slow queries 1 hour predict What could go wrong in the next 24h? — deep-dive Full health sweep with extended context 24 hours silent-failures Find quietly degrading services — change-risk Assess risk from recent deployments 24 hours blast-radius Map dependency chains and cascade risk —

Capabilities that accept a lookback window can be customized: neubird run health 4h, neubird run cost 7d.

neubird investigate "<prompt>" is an alias for neubird run investigate "<prompt>".

docs.title: Flags
docs.text: Flag Default Description --project — Project to investigate (name or UUID). Required on first call. --timeout 120 Investigation timeout in seconds (health/cost/deep-dive enforce 300s minimum) --session — Session file for multi-turn conversations (path or directory) --cleanup false Delete a session file and exit --verbose false Show tool calls, progress markers, and MCP server logs on stderr --format markdown Output format --profile unnamed Login profile (set via global neubird --profile <name>)

docs.title: Multi-turn sessions
docs.text:
Use --session to persist conversation history across invocations, enabling follow-up questions:

# First turn — auto-generates session file in /tmp/
neubird run health --project prod_cop --session /tmp/
# stderr: Session: /tmp/nb-1743620000000.json

# Follow-up — agent has full context from the health sweep
neubird investigate "drill into the RDS memory alarm" --session /tmp/nb-1743620000000.json

# Clean up
neubird investigate --cleanup --session /tmp/nb-1743620000000.json

Session files store conversation history and cached schema context. Follow-up calls skip schema discovery, saving ~15-20 seconds. The --project flag is inherited from the session on follow-ups.

When --session points to a directory, a new session file (nb-<timestamp>.json) is auto-generated. The resolved path is printed to stderr so callers can capture it.

docs.title: Discovering projects
docs.text:
Use neubird projects to list available projects for the current login profile:

neubird projects

PROJECT        ID
prod_cop       ed9e59e3-a843-4a14-8afd-8e3975aef71d
staging_auto   11598cd2-fd50-49c7-8b57-02de7ab1d689
dev_cop        a322dffc-476f-4e5d-8669-fe7e5044dd4c

Both the project name and UUID work with --project.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 Investigation complete, findings on stdout 1 Investigation failed or timed out 2 Not authenticated — run neubird login 3 No connected environment found

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Authenticate — loads credentials from the saved login profile
  2. Connect — connects to the specified project via NeuBird's ACE engine
  3. Discover — scans the project's telemetry schema (cached in session files for follow-ups)
  4. Investigate — runs the same agentic investigation loop as the interactive TUI
  5. Report — prints structured markdown findings to stdout

The investigation uses the same AI engine, tools, and skills as interactive sessions. For health and cost sweeps, findings are handed off to a senior-level synthesis pass before output. See Agentic Investigations for details on how the investigation loop works.

docs.title: Example invocations
docs.text:
# Infrastructure health
neubird run health --project prod_cop
neubird run health 4h --project prod_cop

# Cost analysis
neubird run cost --project prod_cop
neubird run cost 7d --project staging_auto

# Free-form investigation
neubird investigate "the checkout service is throwing 503s" --project prod_cop
neubird investigate "pods in payments namespace are CrashLoopBackOff" --project staging_auto

# Predictive and risk analysis
neubird run predict --project prod_cop
neubird run change-risk --project prod_cop
neubird run silent-failures --project prod_cop

docs.title: Health Sweeps
docs.text: The /health command runs a comprehensive infrastructure health check, scanning across incidents, alarms, error logs, metrics, and recent deployments to produce a structured report.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
/health          # 1-hour lookback (default)
/health 4h       # 4-hour lookback
/health 24h      # Full day
/health 15m      # Quick 15-minute check

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text: Category Data Sources What NeuBird Looks For Incidents PagerDuty, OpsGenie, ServiceNow Active incidents, severity, acknowledgment status Alarms CloudWatch, Datadog monitors Currently firing alarms, alarm history Error logs Grafana Loki, Splunk Error rate by service, new error patterns Metrics Prometheus, CloudWatch, Datadog Resource saturation, latency trends, anomalies Deployments GitHub, GitLab, ArgoCD Recent merges, deployment status, risky changes

docs.title: Report structure
docs.text:
The health report is organized into severity-ranked sections:

Section Description Bad Active problems with evidence, blast radius, and timeline Good Services operating normally, with evidence to prove it Ugly Not broken yet, but trending the wrong way Recommended Actions Prioritized next steps ranked by urgency

Each finding includes the specific data sources and queries that produced the evidence.

docs.title: Agentic Investigations
docs.text: NeuBird doesn't just answer questions — it investigates. Each question triggers an autonomous investigation loop where NeuBird explores your telemetry schema, queries data across multiple sources, correlates the results, and iterates until it reaches a confident conclusion.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Schema discovery — NeuBird searches your telemetry inventory for relevant data sources using pattern matching across all schemas.
  2. Query execution — It queries your telemetry data through a unified access layer, often running multiple queries in parallel across different data sources.
  3. Evidence correlation — Results from different data sources (incidents, metrics, logs, traces) are correlated to build a complete picture.
  4. Iterative refinement — If initial queries don't provide enough information, NeuBird automatically explores further — checking related tables, adjusting time windows, or drilling into specific services.
  5. Synthesis — Once enough evidence is gathered, NeuBird produces a structured analysis with findings, evidence citations, and recommended actions.

docs.title: Real-time visibility
docs.text:
Every step of the investigation is visible in the terminal:

  • Tool calls show which tables are being queried and why
  • Progress bar tracks the investigation phase (exploring → investigating → analyzing → synthesizing)
  • Confidence indicator shows how certain NeuBird is about its current hypothesis

Press Ctrl+O to expand any tool call and inspect the raw query and results. See Tool Review for details.

docs.title: Example questions
docs.text:
• "What services have the highest error rates right now?"
  • "Why did latency spike on api-gateway at 2am?"
  • "What changed in the last 24 hours that could explain the increase in 503s?"
  • "Which deployments correlate with the performance degradation?"

docs.title: Persistent Learning
docs.text: NeuBird gets smarter the more you use it. It accumulates two types of knowledge across sessions, stored server-side in ConfigDB and scoped to the project, so everyone working on that deployment shares one set of learnings.

docs.title: SQL Learnings
docs.text:
When a SQL query fails — for example, because a specific function isn't supported by your database's Foreign Data Wrapper — NeuBird saves a rule about what doesn't work. On subsequent sessions, these rules are injected into the system prompt so NeuBird avoids repeating the same mistakes.

Example: If SELECT date_trunc('hour', timestamp) fails on a particular FDW, NeuBird learns to use an alternative like date_trunc with a different syntax or a workaround. Next time it encounters a similar query, it gets it right on the first try.

Learnings are saved automatically when queries fail. View accumulated learnings with /learnings.

docs.title: Table Learnings
docs.text:
At the end of each successful investigation, NeuBird records which tables contained the most useful data for that type of question. On future investigations, it can skip the schema exploration phase and go directly to the relevant tables.

Example: After investigating "What services have the highest error rates?", NeuBird learns that trace_grafana_tempo.service_map and log_grafana_loki.logs were the key tables. Next time someone asks about error rates, it queries those tables first instead of searching the entire schema.

Table learnings are saved automatically. A maximum of 50 entries are kept, with older entries rotated out.

docs.title: How it improves over time
docs.text: Session Behavior First use Full schema exploration on every question. Some queries may fail on FDW limitations. After a few sessions NeuBird skips known-bad SQL patterns. Starts going directly to useful tables for repeat investigation types. Regular use Investigations are faster and more accurate. Schema exploration is minimal. FDW quirks are fully mapped.

docs.title: Managing learnings
docs.text:
Command Description /learnings View all accumulated SQL learnings /reset Clear conversation history (does not clear learnings)

Learnings persist across sessions in ConfigDB (ace.sql_learnings, ace.table_learnings), written and read through ACE's memory tools. Nothing is kept on the machine running the CLI: a run without an ACE session still learns within that run, but drops what it learned at exit.

docs.title: Predictive Analysis
docs.text: NeuBird doesn't just react to incidents — it helps you see them coming. Ask about risk, degradation trends, or capacity limits, and NeuBird queries your telemetry to identify what's most likely to page you next.

docs.title: What you can ask
docs.text:
Degradation forecasting:

> Based on current trends, what services are at risk of degrading in the next 24 hours?

NeuBird checks latency percentiles, error rate trajectories, resource saturation, traffic growth, and dependency health to tell you where capacity runs out first.

Blast radius analysis:

> If the primary RDS instance goes down, what's the blast radius?

NeuBird traces service dependencies, checks which services depend on the database, and maps the failure cascade.

Risk assessment:

> What's quietly degrading that could page me tonight?

NeuBird looks for silent signals — slowly climbing memory usage, connection pool exhaustion, disk fill rates, error rates that are elevated but not yet alarming.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Predictive analysis uses the same agentic investigation engine as reactive investigations. The difference is the question — instead of asking "what happened?", you're asking "what's about to happen?"

NeuBird:

  1. Queries current metrics and compares against historical baselines
  2. Identifies trends that are moving in the wrong direction
  3. Projects when thresholds will be breached at current rates
  4. Cross-references with recent changes (deploys, config changes) that could be contributing
  5. Ranks risks by severity and time-to-impact

docs.title: Example scenarios
docs.text: Question What NeuBird checks "What services are at risk in the next 24h?" Latency trends, error rates, resource saturation, capacity headroom "What happens if Redis goes down?" Service dependency map, connection counts, failover configuration "Are there any capacity cliffs approaching?" Disk fill rates, connection pool usage, memory trends, ACU utilization "What's the riskiest thing in production right now?" Combines all signals — incidents, alarms, metrics, recent changes

docs.title: Preventive Analysis
docs.text: Don't wait for alerts. NeuBird can proactively scan your infrastructure for issues before they become incidents — and analyze code changes before they reach production.

docs.title: Proactive health checks
docs.text:
Run /health regularly to catch problems while they're still cheap to fix:

> /health

NeuBird scans incidents, alarms, error logs, metrics, and recent deployments to produce a structured Good/Bad/Ugly report. See Health Sweeps for details.

docs.title: Pre-deployment risk analysis
docs.text:
Ask NeuBird to evaluate what could go wrong before merging or deploying a change:

> What pending PRs or recent merges are most likely to cause problems?

NeuBird cross-references code changes with production telemetry — checking current load, historical incidents, related services, and dependency health — then tells you which changes look risky and why.

More examples:

> We're deploying a new version of the payment service — what should we watch for?

> What could break if we scale down the worker pool from 10 to 5 replicas?

> The auth service is getting a major refactor in PR #412 — what production signals should we baseline before merging?

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
NeuBird uses the same investigation engine for preventive analysis as it does for reactive incident response. The difference is timing — you're asking the questions before something breaks, not after.

For code change analysis, NeuBird:

  1. Queries recent PRs and merges from your GitHub/GitLab integration
  2. Identifies which services and components are affected
  3. Checks current production health for those services (error rates, latency, resource usage)
  4. Looks at historical incidents involving the same services
  5. Assesses risk based on change scope, service criticality, and current production state

docs.title: When to use preventive analysis
docs.text: Scenario What to ask Before a deploy "What's the current health baseline for the payment service?" During a change freeze review "What risky changes merged in the last 48 hours?" Monday morning check "/health 72h" (weekend lookback) Before scaling changes "What happens to latency if we reduce replica count?" Release readiness "Are there any silent failures or degradation trends we should address before the release?"

docs.title: Collapsible Tool Output
docs.text: Press Ctrl+O after an investigation completes to enter tool review mode. This lets you inspect every tool call and its results — expand individual calls to see the raw data returned by your telemetry sources, or collapse them to focus on the analysis.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Run an investigation (ask a question or use a slash command)
  2. After the investigation completes, press Ctrl+O
  3. Use ↑ ↓ to navigate between tool calls
  4. Press Enter to expand/collapse a tool call
  5. Press Ctrl+O or Esc to exit review mode

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
Each tool call shows:

  • Tool name — which tool was used (e.g., list_incidents, describe_table, search_tables_regex)
  • Reason — why NeuBird chose to run this query
  • Input — the query parameters or search pattern
  • Output — the raw results (JSON) returned by the data source
  • Learned rules — if NeuBird has learned something about your data source (shown in yellow), such as "never use fired_time in alert_history — describe table first"

Failed or exploratory queries are automatically hidden in the collapsed view but visible when expanded. This is how NeuBird's exploratory probes work — it tries queries that might fail and adapts based on what it learns.

docs.title: A note on the query language
docs.text:
You'll notice that tool calls in the TUI show queries that look like SQL. NeuBird uses SQL as a universal data access layer — a common language for querying across all your telemetry sources. Behind the scenes, these queries are translated by Foreign Data Wrappers into native API calls for each data source:

What you see in the TUI What actually happens SELECT * FROM pagerduty_prod.incidents PagerDuty REST API call SELECT * FROM metric_datadog.cpu_utilization Datadog Metrics API query SELECT * FROM alarm_aws_prod.alarm AWS CloudWatch DescribeAlarms SELECT * FROM trace_grafana_tempo.spans Tempo TraceQL query SELECT * FROM log_grafana_loki.logs Loki LogQL query

This means you don't need to know SQL — NeuBird handles the query generation. The SQL is shown for transparency so you can see exactly what data NeuBird is accessing during an investigation.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Tool review gives you full transparency into NeuBird's reasoning:

  • Verify findings — check that the right data sources were queried and the results support the conclusions
  • Understand the investigation — see which telemetry sources NeuBird found useful and what order it explored them
  • Debug unexpected results — if an investigation produces something unexpected, expand the tool calls to find where the reasoning diverged
  • Share evidence — the raw data backing each finding is right there, ready to copy and share with teammates

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: NeuBird Terminal is distributed as a single binary. Choose the method that suits your environment.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
NeuBird Terminal uses your own LLM credentials — it does not ship with a key. Set one of the following before launching it.

Anthropic:

export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...

AWS Bedrock:

export BEDROCK_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=...
export BEDROCK_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
export BEDROCK_AWS_REGION=us-west-2      # default

Or, with token-based authentication, BEDROCK_API_KEY instead of the two access-key variables.

The provider is auto-detected from whichever credentials are present; set LLM_PROVIDER to anthropic or bedrock to choose explicitly. See Environment Variables for the full list.

You also need a NeuBird account on your organization's deployment (https://yourcompany.app.neubird.ai) — ask your administrator if you do not have one. Connections to your telemetry sources are configured there, not in the terminal.

docs.title: Homebrew (macOS / Linux)
docs.text:
brew install neubirdai/tap/neubird-terminal

Upgrade:

brew upgrade neubird-terminal

docs.title: Snap (Linux)
docs.text: sudo snap install neubird-terminal

docs.title: Debian / Ubuntu
docs.text:
Release assets are version-stamped, so resolve the current version first:

VERSION=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/neubirdai/neubird-terminal/releases/latest \
  | sed -n 's/.*"tag_name": *"v*\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')
: "${VERSION:?could not resolve the latest release; check https://github.com/neubirdai/neubird-terminal/releases}"
curl -fLO "https://github.com/neubirdai/neubird-terminal/releases/download/v${VERSION}/neubird_${VERSION}_linux_amd64.deb"
sudo dpkg -i "neubird_${VERSION}_linux_amd64.deb"

Replace amd64 with arm64 on 64-bit ARM.

docs.title: RPM (Fedora / RHEL / CentOS)
docs.text:
VERSION=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/neubirdai/neubird-terminal/releases/latest \
  | sed -n 's/.*"tag_name": *"v*\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')
: "${VERSION:?could not resolve the latest release; check https://github.com/neubirdai/neubird-terminal/releases}"
curl -fLO "https://github.com/neubirdai/neubird-terminal/releases/download/v${VERSION}/neubird_${VERSION}_linux_amd64.rpm"
sudo rpm -i "neubird_${VERSION}_linux_amd64.rpm"

Replace amd64 with arm64 on 64-bit ARM.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
docker pull neubirdai/neubird-terminal:latest

Run interactively:

docker run -it --rm neubirdai/neubird-terminal:latest

docs.title: Binary download
docs.text:
Pre-built binaries for macOS, Linux, and Windows are available on the releases page.

Asset names include the version, shown here as <version> (for example neubird_1.0.102_darwin_arm64.tar.gz).

Platform Architecture File macOS Apple Silicon neubird_<version>_darwin_arm64.tar.gz macOS Intel neubird_<version>_darwin_amd64.tar.gz Linux x86_64 neubird_<version>_linux_amd64.tar.gz Linux ARM64 neubird_<version>_linux_arm64.tar.gz Windows x86_64 neubird_<version>_windows_amd64.zip Windows ARM64 neubird_<version>_windows_arm64.zip

On macOS and Linux, download the tarball for your platform and move the binary onto your PATH. <version> in the table above is a placeholder; these commands resolve it for you:

VERSION=$(curl -fsSL https://api.github.com/repos/neubirdai/neubird-terminal/releases/latest \
  | sed -n 's/.*"tag_name": *"v*\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p')
: "${VERSION:?could not resolve the latest release}"

ASSET="neubird_${VERSION}_darwin_arm64.tar.gz"   # pick your row from the table
curl -fLO "https://github.com/neubirdai/neubird-terminal/releases/download/v${VERSION}/${ASSET}"
tar -xzf "$ASSET"
sudo mv neubird /usr/local/bin/

On Windows, expand the .zip and put neubird.exe on your PATH:

$tag = (Invoke-RestMethod "https://api.github.com/repos/neubirdai/neubird-terminal/releases/latest").tag_name
$version = $tag.TrimStart("v")
# amd64 on standard PCs, arm64 on Snapdragon / Copilot+ PCs (native and 32-bit shells report ARM64 machines correctly; an x64-emulated shell gets amd64, which still runs)
$arch = if ($env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITECTURE -eq "ARM64" -or $env:PROCESSOR_ARCHITEW6432 -eq "ARM64") { "arm64" } else { "amd64" }
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://github.com/neubirdai/neubird-terminal/releases/download/$tag/neubird_${version}_windows_${arch}.zip" -OutFile neubird.zip
Expand-Archive neubird.zip -DestinationPath "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\NeuBird"

# Current session only
$env:Path += ";$env:LOCALAPPDATA\NeuBird"

# Persist for future sessions
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "$([Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','User'));$env:LOCALAPPDATA\NeuBird", "User")

docs.title: Verify installation

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
This guide walks you through connecting NeuBird Terminal to your account and running your first investigation.

Before you start, make sure you have set an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or Bedrock credentials, and that you know your deployment URL. See Installation → Prerequisites.

docs.title: Step 1: Log in
docs.text:
neubird login https://yourcompany.app.neubird.ai

NeuBird prompts for your email and password:

Username/Email: alice@yourcompany.com
Password: ********

Your credentials are saved locally. You only need to log in once.

docs.title: Step 2: Launch
docs.text:
neubird

NeuBird connects to your telemetry environment, discovers your schemas, and drops you into the interactive terminal. You'll see context-aware welcome tiles — starter investigations tailored to your data sources.

Use ← → to browse tiles, or just start typing a question.

docs.title: Step 3: Ask a question
docs.text:
Type any question and press Enter:

> What services have the highest error rates right now?

NeuBird queries your telemetry data, shows each tool call as it runs, and produces a written analysis with evidence and recommended actions.

docs.title: Step 4: Run a health sweep
docs.text:
/health

This runs a full infrastructure health check with a 1-hour lookback window and produces a structured Good/Bad/Ugly report. Use /health 4h for a longer window.

docs.title: Agent Personas
docs.text: NeuBird includes three built-in agent personas, each using a different Claude model tuned for a different trade-off between speed and depth.

docs.title: Personas
docs.text:
Persona Model Speed Quality Best for Responder claude-haiku-4-5 ⚡⚡⚡ ★☆☆ Fast triage, immediate next actions Analyst claude-sonnet-5 ⚡⚡○ ★★☆ Root cause analysis, deep investigation Architect claude-opus-5-5 ⚡○○ ★★★ Runbooks, design reviews, systemic fixes

Switch persona at any time with /agent.

docs.title: Responder
docs.text:
The Responder uses Claude Haiku for maximum speed. It is best for:

  • Confirming whether an incident is ongoing
  • Getting an immediate triage summary
  • Identifying the next action to take

docs.title: Analyst
docs.text:
The Analyst uses Claude Sonnet for balanced speed and depth. It is the default persona; the main investigation instructions live in agents/Analyst.md (embedded in the binary, overridable on disk). Best for:

  • Full root cause analysis (RCA)
  • Multi-service investigations
  • Latency, error rate, and cost investigations

docs.title: Architect
docs.text:
The Architect uses Claude Opus for maximum reasoning depth. It is best for:

  • Writing runbooks from investigation results
  • Designing systemic fixes
  • Design review questions that require reasoning over multiple investigations

docs.title: Custom personas
docs.text:
You can add your own agent personas as .md files in skills/agents/. The frontmatter sets the model, speed, and quality rating; the body is appended to the system prompt.

Example: skills/agents/cost-specialist.md

---
model: claude-sonnet-5
speed: 2
quality: 2
---

You are a cloud cost specialist. When investigating costs, always break down by service, team, and resource type. Always include a projected monthly cost at the end of your analysis.

docs.text: Key Action ↑ / ↓ Navigate input history Ctrl+R Reverse-search through input history ← / → Navigate welcome tiles Enter Submit input or select tile (typed text always takes priority over tile selection) Esc Cancel in-progress investigation / deselect tile focus Tab Accept autocomplete suggestion or complete a slash command Ctrl+C twice Quit ? Toggle the keyboard shortcut overlay

docs.title: Slash Commands
docs.text: Type a slash command in the input bar and press Enter (or Tab to autocomplete).

docs.title: Investigation & analysis
docs.text: Command Description /health Infrastructure health sweep with 1-hour lookback. Produces a Good/Bad/Ugly summary. /health <window> Health sweep with a custom lookback window. Examples: /health 15m, /health 4h, /health 24h /cost Cloud cost analysis with 24-hour spend projection. /cost <window> Cost analysis with a custom lookback window. Example: /cost 7d /sentinel Start sentinel mode — continuous background alert monitoring. /sentinel off Stop sentinel mode. /sentinel status Show sentinel status and active findings.

docs.title: Environment & connections
docs.text: Command Description /agent Switch SRE agent persona. Opens an interactive picker. /tables List all telemetry tables available in the connected database. /project Switch to a different database. /config Show current connection info. /config clear Clear the saved database selection. /mcp Show MCP server status. /tools Show all available tools. /learnings Show SQL learnings from past investigations. /skills List available skills (built-in and installed).

docs.title: Output & session
docs.text: Command Description /export Export the current answer (interactive format picker). /copy Copy the current answer to clipboard. /welcome Show the welcome screen with investigation tiles. /help Show help. /reset Clear the current conversation history. NeuBird starts fresh on the next question. /clear Clear the display. History is preserved. /quit Exit NeuBird Terminal.

docs.title: Custom slash commands
docs.text:
You can add your own slash commands as Markdown files in the skills/ directory (or the directory set by HAWKEYE_SKILLS_DIR).

The filename (without .md) becomes the command name. A top-level # heading in the file becomes the command description shown in the autocomplete menu. The file body is injected into the conversation as a user message when the command is invoked.

Example: create skills/weekend-check.md:

# Weekend incident check

Review the last 48 hours of telemetry and summarize any anomalies or incidents that occurred over the weekend.

This makes /weekend-check available as a slash command.

docs.title: Managing skills
docs.text:
NeuBird Terminal can install skills from the FalconClaw skills registry. Use the neubird skills CLI to browse and manage them.

Command Description neubird skills list List installed skills. neubird skills search <query> Search the skills registry. neubird skills install <name> Install a skill from the registry. neubird skills remove <name> Remove an installed skill.

Installed skills are stored in ~/.config/neubird/skills/ and are automatically available as slash commands.

docs.title: Terminal UI
docs.text: NeuBird Terminal runs as a full-screen terminal application built on Bubbletea.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
When you connect, the TUI shows:

  • Welcome tiles — context-aware starter questions based on your telemetry schema. Use ← → to navigate, Enter to select.
  • Input bar — type any question or slash command and press Enter to submit.
  • Investigation panel — NeuBird streams its analysis here as it runs, showing tool activity, data source queries, and the final answer.
  • Status bar — current connection info, active agent persona, and data sources used in the last investigation.

docs.title: Input history
docs.text: NeuBird remembers your previous inputs. Use ↑ / ↓ to navigate history, or Ctrl+R to search it.

docs.title: Cancelling an investigation
docs.text: Press Esc to cancel an in-progress investigation. The model stops at the next safe point.

docs.title: Quitting
docs.text: Press Ctrl+C twice, or type /quit.

docs.title: Dark and light terminal support
docs.text: The TUI adapts its color palette to your terminal's background. No configuration required.

docs.title: Session persistence
docs.text: NeuBird saves your last-used database selection in ~/.config/neubird/state.json and restores it on the next run.
